- The intermediate school board must submit its proposed General Fund budget to each constituent district by May 1 each year.

- The Secretary (or designee) shall forward the resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent by June 1.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A blank template of the "Support for General Fund Budget" resolution — labeled "ISD BUDGET RESOLUTION" — that a constituent district's board of education uses to express support for its intermediate school district's proposed General Fund budget. The filename ties it to the FY27 Oakland Schools (OS) General Fund budget support resolution. All identifying fields are left as fill-in-the-blank placeholders: the district name; the meeting type, location, day, month, and time; the president calling the meeting to order; the members present and absent; and the members offering and supporting the resolution.

The recited preamble tracks Section 624 of the Revised School Code, as amended: the intermediate school board must submit its proposed General Fund budget no later than May 1 each year to the board of each constituent district for review; and no later than June 1 each year, each constituent district's board must review the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget, adopt a resolution expressing support or disapproval, and submit any specific objections and proposed changes to the intermediate school board.

The operative language resolves that: (1) the board has received and reviewed the proposed intermediate school district General Fund budget under Section 624 and expresses its support; (2) the secretary or designee shall forward a copy of the resolution to the intermediate school board or its superintendent no later than June 1; and (3) all conflicting resolutions are rescinded. Ayes/Nays member lines, a "Resolution declared adoption" line, and a Secretary's certification block (referencing the Open Meetings Act, 1976 PA 267, as amended) follow, all with blanks to be completed. This generic form is the template underlying the meeting's adopted Item 5.I. Oakland ISD General Fund budget resolution.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A Scope of Services proposal from EL Education, a K-12 education non-profit, outlining professional development to support Troy School District's FY27 pilot of the EL Education 6-8 Language Arts curriculum. The plan spans four middle schools and bundles strategic planning, a two-part Teacher Pilot Launch (August 19 and October 30), virtual office hours, and in-person and virtual coaching days. The priced items total $5,000 for the in-person launch, with several services (valued at roughly $6,000 to $13,200 each) provided gratis.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A FY27 pilot Scope of Services proposal from EL Education, a national K-12 non-profit, for professional development supporting Troy School District's implementation of the EL Education 6-8 English Language Arts curriculum across four middle schools.

Services and pricing
- Strategic Planning: 2 days of facilitated 60-90 minute sessions with the District Leadership Team; gratis ($6,000 priced)
- 6-8 ELA Teacher Pilot Launch: half-day sessions on August 19 and October 30; $5,000 (in person)
- Virtual Office Hours with teachers and coaches: 4-6 sessions plus a 'Troy School District' landing page of resources; gratis
- 4 Coaching Days during pilot: one day at each of the four piloting middle schools, teachers teach a half day then receive feedback and PD; gratis ($13,200 priced)
- Virtual School-Based Coaching Days: 2 days / 12 hours for office hours, planning, and as-needed support; gratis (about $6,000 priced)

Purpose
To prepare leaders and teachers to implement the 6-8 ELA curriculum, understanding its structure and design, identifying how it targets the literacy achievement gap, and planning High Leverage Instructional Practices. Coaching uses the Qualtrics data platform for progress monitoring and builds capacity among school-based leadership and teacher leaders. The proposal emphasizes meeting national standards, deepening student engagement, and raising student achievement.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
EL Education, a K-12 education non-profit focused on raising achievement in America's public schools, submitted a Scope of Services proposal for Troy School District's FY27 pilot implementation of its 6-8 Language Arts curriculum. EL Education provides multi-year partnerships pairing a rigorous K-8 curriculum with classroom-tested teacher resources, professional learning, strategic planning, and coaching centered on leaders and teachers.

The District Implementation proposal itemizes services and prices for the FY27 pilot:

Strategic Planning: two days facilitated in 60-90-minute collaborative sessions with the District Leadership Team, customized with expert EL Education staff and school/district leaders to inform the partnership plan and monitor implementation goals through in-person meetings plus weekly phone/virtual touchpoints; provided gratis ($6,000 priced).

EL Education 6-8 Language Arts Curriculum Teacher Pilot Launch: half-day sessions on August 19 and October 30 giving teachers an understanding of the curriculum's principles and structure and beginning instructional planning; priced at $5,000 (in person). Stated objectives include describing the structure, design, and key features of the curriculum; identifying specific ways it is designed to close the literacy achievement gap; analyzing the components to begin planning for instruction; and planning to implement High Leverage Instructional Practices that meet all learners' needs.

Virtual Office Hours with teachers and coaches: 4-6 sessions delivering short professional-learning segments and answering questions, scheduled around the middle schools' dynamic schedules with teacher stipends and no need for substitutes, plus a 'Troy School District' landing page linking to resources, videos, and supports; gratis.

Four Coaching Days during the pilot: one day at each of the four piloting middle schools, with teachers teaching a half day and then released for feedback, action steps, and PD for a half day. EL coaches work with school-based instructional leadership, implementation teams, and teachers on professional learning plans and development, data analysis, strategic planning, goal setting, and progress monitoring using the Qualtrics data platform, building the capacity of school-based leadership and teacher leaders; gratis ($13,200 priced).

Virtual School-Based Coaching Days: two days (which can be broken into 12 hours of support) delivered virtually for office hours, planning sessions, and as-needed support aligned to each individual school's goals and data, with the EL coach supporting building leaders on data collection and analysis, teacher observation and feedback conversations, and grade-level planning sessions; gratis (approximately $6,000 priced).

Throughout, the proposal frames its professional services around meeting the higher bar of national standards, deepening student engagement, and transforming teaching and learning to lead to high student achievement.

Proposed total funding is $563.2 million and total expenditures $591.7 million, with property taxes ($270.7 million) and an estimated $200.2 million in grant awards as the largest revenue sources. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Oakland Schools' proposed Original Budget for fiscal year 2026-27, dated 03/24/2026, opens with an enterprise-wide overview of the intermediate school district (ISD) that serves Oakland County, including Troy School District. Oakland Schools is one of 56 ISDs established in Michigan in 1962, an autonomous, tax-supported public school district governed by Michigan General School Law that provides regional support services to constituent districts best delivered regionally by cost, size, and quality. Its mission is 'Every Student. Every Day.'

The overview lays out the organization's beliefs and credo (service, expertise, and excellence; a first responsibility to Oakland County educators, students, and families) and three organizational objectives: increasing student achievement, serving the diverse needs of schools, and decreasing costs while increasing efficiencies.

Funding - proposed total funding of $563.2 million:
- Property taxes: $270.7 million
- Other local revenue and investment revenue: $51.7 million
- State source revenue: $24.8 million
- Other financing sources and indirect revenue: $15.8 million
- Estimated grant award funding: $200.2 million
Funding is presented net of eligible inter-company eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund revenues.

Expenditures - proposed total of $591.7 million:
- Salary, wage, and benefits: $88.8 million
- Purchased services, supplies, utilities and dues/fees: $27.2 million
- Capital outlay: $23.9 million
- Transfers to LEAs and other funds: $233.4 million
- Grant-related expenditures: $200.2 million
- Payment on existing debt: $18.2 million
Expenditures are likewise net of eligible eliminated Risk Related Activity Fund expenses.

Under 'What's New or of Special Significance,' the budget notes that property tax revenue is budgeted to increase by 3.4%, or $9.0 million. Taxable values have increased incrementally over the last twelve years and finally reached pre-recession levels in 2022-23; while Oakland County taxable values are expected to increase just over 4.0%, the District uses a conservative estimate until actual taxable values are available. Tax abatements leveled off for several years after peaking in fiscal years 2012 and 2013, but tax tribunal challenges rose over the last two years, and the District carefully monitors open cases with assistance from Oakland County Equalization, holding reserves for anticipated abatement losses because all unfavorable judgments are the District's responsibility.

The budget separately addresses Michigan Tax Tribunal (MTT) expense: MTT judgments on property tax assessments directly affect Oakland Schools' expenditures because unfavorable judgments result in the return of funds to the taxing authority with no recoupment from the State of Michigan, so the District evaluates the associated risk.

Adjustments

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A background information memo dated 5.13.26 that accompanies the International Academy's 'Revenues by Source and Expenditures by Object' schedule. That schedule compares the recommended Final 2025-26 budget against the original budget adopted in June 2025 and also presents the proposed Original Budget for 2026-27. The memo explains that adopted budgets rest on assumptions, chiefly pupil enrollment and staffing, and require adjustment as those assumptions change.

Governance and approval process: Under the cooperative agreement, Bloomfield (the fiscal agent) provides budgets to the participating local districts, which must approve them through their boards of education by the end of June. An amended 2025-26 budget was approved by the Bloomfield Board of Education at its March 23, 2026 meeting. The Final 2025-26 budget and the Original 2026-27 budget were scheduled to be presented to Bloomfield's BOE for approval on June 15.

Tuition and enrollment: The tuition rate charged to districts follows the State's target foundation allowance plus ten percent. For 2025-26 the rate is $11,055, and enrollment as of the October count date used for billing is 576 students, a decrease of 5 compared to 2024-25, with adjusted revenue consistent with the adopted budget. Bloomfield is also recognizing the amount of state Section 27l funds distributed to Bloomfield educators, which has no impact on fund balance because the revenue recognized equals the total of 27l costs (wage payment and related benefits). For 2026-27 the assumed tuition rate is $11,330, reflecting a $250 per-pupil foundation increase plus ten percent, and enrollment is projected at 590, an increase of 14 over 2025-26, attributed to a larger incoming freshman class.

Expenditure adjustments: For 2025-26, expenditures were increased from the original budget by over $200,000, primarily to account for salaries and benefits tied to contracts negotiated and settled after the original budget was adopted in March 2025, which vary by district; additionally, the expected value of attrition savings from two retirements at the end of 2024-25 did not occur as anticipated. For 2026-27, expenditures were adjusted to reflect known on-scale wage increases and to account for attrition savings from two educators whose positions will not be filled; an average retirement rate of 26.5% was used for the projection. The memo notes that 'payments to other school districts' represent the cost of each local district's payroll and benefits for its teachers assigned to the International Academy, and likewise include known on-scale increases as well as a reduced retirement rate.

In total, the four pilots are summarized as costing $1,093,710 from the district's 35m grant allocation and $63,939.09 from general funds (the sum of the Arts and Letters $36,304.59, EL Education $5,000, and Kiddom $22,634.50 amounts). The memo closes by inviting questions and references an attached Purchase Summary. Read alongside the other May 19, 2026 board materials, it ties together the Center for the Collaborative Classroom quote (Being a Reader), the EL Education scope of services, and the Kiddom order form into a single funding recommendation for elementary and middle-school literacy pilots.

Minutes of a regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held Tuesday, April 21, 2026 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. All seven board members were present: Anne, Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Smotherman, Brennan, Griffin, Algeier, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Approximately 75 members of the public attended. The Pledge of Allegiance was recited.

Outstanding Teachers of the Year: The Board recognized its 2026 Outstanding Teachers of the Year. More than 49 Troy School District educators were nominated, and three were selected based on passion, dedication, impact, and excellence in teaching. A video was shown of the administrative team surprising each winner in their classroom. The three recipients are Lindsey Maliepaard, Elementary Teacher of the Year from Costello Elementary School; Tammy Gilbert, Middle School Teacher of the Year from Boulan Park Middle School; and Christina Rick of Troy High School, named both High School and Overall Teacher of the Year. All three were submitted to Oakland Schools to represent Troy in the countywide Outstanding Teacher Award program, and Christina Rick was named the 2026 Oakland County High School Teacher of the Year. The Board announced a reception for all nominees on Wednesday, April 29 at Troy High School, where each nominee would receive a certificate, their nomination materials, and a token of appreciation. Each of the three winners was invited to the podium to speak and take a photo with the Board.

TSD Mission Moment — Shamrock Shakedown: The Board highlighted the 'Shamrock Shakedown,' a school-wide basketball tradition at the Troy Center for Transition (TCT) that began as a shared passion for basketball between students and staff and grew into an event celebrating teamwork, inclusion, and community. International Academy East (IA East) partners on the event, leading game-day setup and serving as master of ceremonies, with a dynamic soundtrack and halftime performances. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski introduced their students; Ava Pittman from IA-East and Nathan Kohnert from TCT described their experience participating in the event and shared a brief video.

Autism Acceptance Month: April was designated Autism Acceptance Month, and the Board took up a resolution to celebrate the contributions of neurodiverse people and work toward ending disparities. The motion was made by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Alic. The resolution's recitals state that Autism Spectrum Disorder affects more than five million people in the United States; that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report 1 in 36 children may have autism; that autism is a neurological and developmental disorder characterized by social impairment and restricted interactive and communication behaviors that can affect anyone regardless of race, ethnicity, gender, or socioeconomic background; and that physicians, psychologists, behavior analysts, speech and language pathologists, occupational therapists, vocational rehabilitation professionals, and educators can assist individuals with autism and their families through early identification, education, and intervention. The extracted text is truncated within this resolution before a vote is recorded, and any subsequent agenda items are not captured.

A transmittal letter dated March 25, 2026 from Kenneth Gutman, Superintendent of Oakland Schools, addressed to constituent-district Board of Education designates (including the Troy School District), inviting review of the proposed Oakland Schools budget for FY 2026-27. Per the Michigan School Code, Section 380.624(2), the proposed FY 2026-27 General Fund budget is submitted to constituent district Boards of Education for review; Oakland Schools includes all of its fund budgets for transparency, but constituent districts vote only on the General Fund budget.

Revenue: Oakland Schools is primarily funded by property-tax dollars, and the intermediate district projects a growth factor in its property-tax revenues of 3.4%. Tax-revenue projections are described as conservative relative to Oakland County taxable-value increase projections, since actual taxable-value figures are not available during budget preparation.

Key projects and initiatives referenced in the Enterprise-Wide Executive Summary include: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Strategy and Capacity Building; a Special Populations Continuum of Supports; Social-Emotional Wellbeing and Mental Health Support; a Nanotechnology, Artificial Intelligence and Synthetic Biology (NAIS) Lab; Oakland Schools Technical Campus renovations; a Business Office Residency Program; a Human Resources Leadership Academy (HRLA); the Essential Practices in Instruction — Capacity & Coherence (EPIC) Numeracy Project; and Literacy Essentials Oakland (LEO).

Subsidies: Oakland Schools provides over $1.4 million in subsidies for software and other instructional tools in Career and Technical Education and in curriculum and assessment, exclusive of pass-through grant funds, other district allocations, and the cost of dedicated support staff.

Personnel costs: The 2026-27 budget includes step increases for eligible employees along with a 2.0% salary increase for all staff; all union salary changes, including step adjustments, are subject to collective bargaining.

PA-18 Special Education Funding: Oakland Schools receives property-tax revenue to support special-education programs. The base distribution of PA-18 funding to local districts is budgeted to increase approximately $5.2 million, or 2.9%. An additional $2.5 million is budgeted for other LEA distributions covering group-home expenditures, reimbursements to districts for educating incarcerated youth, special-education program startup, extraordinary expenditures, and capital. The budget also contains $5.0 million for construction of an Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) Center Program in Oxford. In FY 2025-26, Oakland Schools distributed additional PA-18 funds totaling $5.8 million above the base distribution.

Planning: Oakland Schools uses a five-year forecast updated with each budget amendment (incorporating projections from Oakland County Equalization for taxable values) and maintains an annually updated five-year capital plan for facility and equipment improvements.

Process and timing: The proposed General Fund budget is to be submitted to constituent districts by May 1, and each district's board must adopt a resolution of support or non-support not later than June 1. A presentation to the 28 local district business managers was scheduled at the Oakland County School Business Officials meeting on April 17, 2026, followed by a Designates Meeting on April 29 at 6:00 PM, giving local board designates and district administration an opportunity to review the General Fund budget before submitting their resolution by June 1, 2026. The Oakland Schools Board of Education will hold a Truth in Budgeting hearing on June 1 and consider the FY 2026-27 proposed budget documents for approval during its regular meeting that night. Questions are directed to the superintendent's office at 248.209.2424. The letter is signed by Kenneth Gutman, Superintendent.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum on Troy School District Technology Services letterhead (4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.5060) addressed to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, from Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology, regarding an Apple Purchase. The memo is dated April 30, 2024 and carries an approval request of $2,420,430 to purchase 4,400 total devices for a comprehensive refresh of both student and staff technology across the district.

Student devices ($1,017,480): 2,400 iPads for incoming grades 2, 4, and 10, replacing all end-of-life 7th generation iPads. Associated actions include repurposing about 400 9th generation iPads from Grade 10 to Kindergarten and testing carts, reassigning current Grade 2 cart devices to Grade 3, and selling surplus 9th generation iPads to maximize value.

Staff devices ($1,402,950): 1,000 M5 MacBook Airs and 1,000 latest-generation iPads, replacing aging M1 MacBook Airs and end-of-life 7th generation staff iPads while maintaining a 5-year refresh cycle. The district plans to retain limited MacBooks for substitute/backup use and sell the remaining devices to offset cost.

Financial overview: Total estimated resale recovery of $497,600-$565,600 yields an estimated net cost of $1.85M-$1.92M. A cost table lists Student iPads (2,400 units, $1,017,480, ~$423 average), Staff Devices (2,000 units, $1,402,950, ~$701 average), and Total (4,400 units, $2,420,430, ~$550 average). A resale table estimates recovery by device type: 7th Gen iPads (3,200 units at $60-$70 each, $192K-$224K), 9th Gen iPads (800 units at $82-$92 each, $65.6K-$73.6K), and M1 MacBook Air 2020 (800 units at $300-$335 each, $240K-$268K).

Stated outcomes: eliminating all end-of-life 7th generation devices; improving performance, reliability, and user experience; maximizing value through repurposing and resale; supporting instructional consistency and operational efficiency; and reducing future refresh costs through strategic lifecycle management. Vasovski recommends approval to proceed with the investment to maintain a modern, secure, and high-performing technology environment for both students and staff. (The memo body is dated April 30, 2024, while the associated Apple quote and workshop fall in mid-2026.)

Chartwells, the Troy School District's contracted Food and Nutrition Services vendor, presented this board report and strategic plan at the Board of Education Workshop on June 1, 2026. The presenters were Gayle Moran, the district's Food Service Liaison (gmoran@troy.k12.mi.us); Nicole Gervais, Chartwells Food Service Director (ngervais@troy.k12.mi.us); and Debbie Elzerman, Chartwells Area Director (Deborah.Elzerman@compass-usa.com).

The report frames a 'Path Forward to Increase Lunch Participation' organized around student meal programs at the secondary level (2026-2027), the 'Nutrition: Game On' elementary program (2026-2027), ongoing meal quality and training enhancements, equipment upgrades and a smallwares/cafe refresh in Fall 2026, and enhanced communications.

Meal participation data cited: 6,607 average daily lunches, 2,637 average daily breakfasts, 55% lunch participation, 22% breakfast participation, and 1,471,180 meals served year-to-date. Financial figures include $201,570 in year-to-date a la carte revenue and $98,598 in catering revenue.

The elementary 'Nutrition: Game On' program guides students through monthly quests with featured recipes, movement, storytelling, and hands-on activities. It introduces a cast of characters: Leo and Dani (who lead the monthly quests), Hailey Harvest (where food comes from), Clara Curious (science experiments), Max Motion (physical activity), Mei Market (smart shopping lists), and Chef Sizzle (themed recipe cooking). Program components span signage, overhead and countertop menu boards, engagement lessons and displays, takeaways, food demos, recipe cards, theme menus, and environmental elements such as murals, fixtures, paint, and flooring. Existing programs connect nutrition education and cooking demonstrations with a promotional calendar, an annual middle-school cultural cooking competition, student tasting and voting events, global food exploration, and a farm-to-school elementary program featuring local produce.

Secondary participation drivers include seasonal limited-time promotions for SY26-27 (Winter, August 3 to November 1; Fall, November 2 to January 31; Spring, February 1 to May 2; Summer, May 3 to August 1), home-made specialty pizzas, new strombolis, specialty flatbreads, and dips and seasonings. A featured initiative, 'Power Up Wednesdays,' introduces new protein bowls available at all secondary locations, each substitutable with tofu and/or beans: a Greek Protein Bowl (chicken, chickpeas, rice, cucumbers, tomatoes, feta, yogurt dressing), a Southwest Bowl (shaved beef, black bean and corn salsa, brown rice, peppers, onions, avocado, southwest crema), a BBQ Bowl (diced chicken, black beans, brown rice, corn, cabbage slaw, sweet potatoes, pickles, BBQ sauce), and an Asian Bowl (diced chicken, brown rice, broccoli, water chestnuts, bok choy, radishes, carrots, teriyaki).

To enhance meal quality and communication, Chartwells outlines summer associate trainings including a Welcome Back Orientation, Kitchen Skills and Quality Assurance Training, and a Summer Manager Meeting covering USDA meal pattern requirements, food safety and sanitation, allergy management, production records, menu planning, and ordering. The signature Culinary Masterclass, led by a Chartwells Regional Executive Chef, is K-12 specific with 13 hands-on learning modules emphasizing knife skills, food safety, and scratch-and-batch cooking; all kitchen leads attend June 9 and 10. Communication channels listed include a Youth Advisory Council, social media, monthly newsletters, website information, Nutrislice online menus, and board reports such as this one.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This Troy School District Board of Education presentation, titled Amendment #3 and dated June 2026, reviews the final 2025-2026 budget amendments and the proposed 2026-2027 budget. It accompanies a public hearing addressing truth in taxation and the establishment of millage rates, and covers the General Fund, ancillary funds (2023 Capital Projects, Debt Funds, Building Site and Sinking, Capital Maintenance), and special revenue funds (Food Service, Troy Career Center, Troy Preschool, and School and Student Activities).

Taxable values are shown rising from 2025 to 2026: homestead from $3,657,042,480 to $3,800,792,510, non-homestead from $1,953,185,000 to $2,064,220,210, and total taxable value from $5,610,227,480 to $5,865,012,720. Taxable value increases are capped at the lesser of inflation or 5%. The presentation explains the 6-mill State Education Tax on homestead and non-homestead property, the 18-mill operating millage on non-homestead property, the enrollment-based Hold Harmless millage (2.7294 mills in FY25), and the Sinking Fund (0.9606 mills FY25) and Debt Fund (6.1000 mills) levies, together with the 1978 Headlee Amendment rollback mechanism.

Homestead millage comparisons across 2024-2025, 2025-2026, and 2026-2027 show State Education Tax steady at 6.0000; Hold Harmless declining 2.7294, 2.5796, 2.4102; Debt steady at 6.1000; and Sinking Fund declining 0.9606, 0.9540, 0.9472. Total homestead millage falls 15.7900, 15.6336, 15.4574, and total non-homestead millage falls 31.0606, 31.0540, 31.0472.

General Fund budget adjustments in Amendment #3 reflect anticipated final state categorical aid, federal grant allocations, ISD-related funding, and final purchased-services, salary, and benefit expenditures. The 2026-2027 proposed budget assumes the lowest categorical and foundation allowance figures among the Governor, House, and Senate proposals; a blended FTE count of 11,869 (down from the current 12,069); a minimum foundation allowance increase of $250 per pupil; and a target of $12 million in general fund expenditure reductions.

Budget priorities include securing known expenditure obligations through 2029 to enable multi-year projections and labor stability, data-driven alignment of student support services (K-12 MTSS teams, a K-8 reading curriculum, and continued math implementation), and reductions through attrition, noting that 95% of the budget is personnel and that any reduction in force would be viewed through least impact on student achievement, with a possible Employee Severance Plan under review. Cited budgetary challenges are enrollment, lack of urgency in Lansing, the revenue landscape, rising expenditures, salaries and benefits, retirement costs, and special education. Reduction targets emphasize maintaining instructional priorities, structural balance, and a 15% fund-balance target, with proposed cuts to salaries and benefits, purchased services, departmental budgets, and discretionary spending, guided by a budget reduction rubric and scoring; candidate areas include non-classroom positions, adult-to-student ratios, and administrative and support staffing realignment.

The General Fund summary compares the 2025-2026 Original Budget, 2025-2026 Amendment #3, and 2026-2027 Proposed Budget: revenue of $190,545,984, $201,962,102, and $192,228,696; expenditures of $194,285,613, $207,549,509, and $194,199,428; change in fund balance of ($3,739,629), ($5,587,407), and ($1,970,732); beginning fund balance of $32,979,691, $33,554,567, and $27,967,160; ending fund balance of $29,240,062, $27,967,160, and $25,996,428; and fund balance percentages of 15.05%, 13.47%, and 13.39%.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document presents the full bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), displayed with proposed amendments highlighted for member-district consideration in spring 2026; a note directs readers to proposed changes on pages 4, 8, and 9. It was included in the Troy School District Board of Education workshop packet of June 1, 2026. The adoption history records adoption by the Board of Directors on 11/15/2017, adoption by the General Membership on 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018, and amendments approved by member school districts on 9/16/2020, 9/10/2021, 3/3/2023, and 6/6/2025.

Article I (Offices) locates the principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, and requires a continuously maintained registered office and agent. Article II (Purpose) lists the association's aims: to advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education; to promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; to make information about educational issues available to board members; to conduct meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; to promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; to enhance cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards; to present a strong, unified force representing school boards' views to political representatives; and to advocate for county, state, and national legislation supporting public education by locally elected boards.

Article III (Membership) makes any publicly elected Oakland County school district board member, or any elected Oakland ISD board member, who is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB), an eligible general member ('Member School Districts'). Section 2 grants each Member one vote per matter, exercised in person, with an exception: each Member School District has one vote on resolutions (Article IX) or to amend the Bylaws (Article XVI), recorded upon receipt of a completed resolution or ballot reflecting the district's trustees' vote, due before the ballot deadline, with results reported to all member districts by the next general membership meeting. Section 3 limits electronic voting to the Board of Directors for emergency business, to be reaffirmed at the next board meeting. Section 4 states membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV (Dues) provides that the association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, by Intermediate School District membership dues not exceeding the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts. Article V (Meeting of Members) requires an annual meeting plus not fewer than three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business; the annual meeting is the first regular meeting after July 1, with dates, times, and places set by the Board of Directors. Special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more Board of Directors members with 30 days' notice, and the document addresses designation of meeting place and valid meetings held by unanimous consent of members.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) document, dated May 2026 and included in the Troy School District Board of Education workshop packet of June 1, 2026, presents a proposed new resolution for member-district consideration and reprints OCSBA's continuing resolutions for reference.

The proposed new resolution states: 'OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege.' The rationale explains that in the FY26 school aid budget, Section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to opt in, and that any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. OCSBA argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass-casualty event is necessary to help prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on the issue, and that nothing would stop the legislature from later tying waiver of the privilege to other funding.

The document notes, per OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, that resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. It then lists continuing resolutions already adopted by member districts, each with adoption and amendment dates and cross-references to MASB resolutions:

- Accountability and Transparency (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports holding every publicly funded school to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, public school academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and colleges and universities (MASB Resolution A 6.65).
- Broadband Access and Devices (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): supports including broadband in infrastructure plans, expanded affordable and reliable access, funding for internet-capable devices and software, and dedicated cybersecurity resources (MASB Resolution A-10.30).
- Early Childhood (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports new dollars for universal public preschool for four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for five-year-olds (MASB Resolution A 6.15).
- Early On Michigan (adopted 1/26/2026): supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at-risk conditions.
- Evidence-Based Decision Making (adopted 9/24/2019; MASB G 11.01); Lame Duck (adopted 9/24/2019); and Local Control (adopted 9/24/2019; MASB A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70), supporting community-governed public schools with elected boards.
- Mental Health (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports increased mental health services and professionals and at-minimum annual inflation-adjusted state resources (MASB G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50).
- Non-Partisan Elections (adopted 1/9/2026): supports non-partisan school board elections.
- School Aid (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): would specify constitutionally that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th-grade public education and oppose private school vouchers or tax-credit programs; support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk, and ELL students; protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes; and enact the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 (MASB Resolutions A 10.25, A 10.05, A 10.55).

Amendment 1 would let the dues-paying Oakland Intermediate School District appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term on the 7-to-9-member Board of Directors under Article VI; the ISD currently pays $6,000 per year in direct dues. Amendment 2 would require that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee be a Board of Directors member, revising Article IX Sections 3 and 4.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
OCSBA proposed bylaws amendments packet for 2026, prepared by the Resolutions & Bylaws Committee and sent to member districts (including Troy) for consideration and vote. Reviewed at the June 1, 2026 Board of Education Workshop.

Amendment 1 - ISD appointed Trustee
- Adds language to Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Section 2 (Eligibility).
- The Intermediate School District, which pays annual dues directly to the Association (currently $6,000/year), would be entitled to appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors.
- If the ISD declines, it must notify the Board in writing within 30 days of a Board election so the seat can be filled by election.
- The one-director-per-district limit and total board size are unchanged.
- Rationale: board continuity for a working board that struggles to fill all 9 seats, plus recognition of ISD in-kind support (event space, AV, advocacy, no-cost speakers) and service agreements the dues offset.

Amendment 2 - committee leadership
- Requires either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee to be a Board of Directors member.
- Revises Article IX, Section 3 (Committee Chairs) and Section 4 (Government Relations Committee).
- If an elected committee chair is not a Director, the Association Board appoints a Director as Vice-Chair.
- Chair elections occur at the first committee meeting after July 1 (after January 31 for the GRC), with at least 7 days' written notice.

Reference
Article VI Section 1 sets the Board of Directors at an odd number, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members (unchanged).
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) Resolutions & Bylaws Committee prepared two proposed bylaws amendments for the 2026 cycle, transmitted to member districts including Troy School District, which reviewed them at its June 1, 2026 Board of Education Workshop.

Proposed Amendment 1 would allow a member district that pays dues directly to the Association to appoint a Trustee to a seat on the Board of Directors, adding new language to Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Section 2 (Eligibility). The provision restates that any Member is eligible for election, with only one Member per Member School District serving at a time. Because the Intermediate School District (ISD) pays annual membership dues directly to the Association, it would be entitled to appoint one (1) Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors. If the ISD chooses not to exercise this right, it must notify the Board of Directors in writing within 30 days of a Board election so the seat can be filled by election. The stated rationale: the ISD is the only member district that also pays annual dues directly (currently $6,000 per year); the appointment supports board continuity for a working Board of Directors that struggles to fill all 9 positions; and it changes neither the one-director-per-district limit nor the total number of directors. The rationale cites the ISD's in-kind support, including event space with AV equipment and staff, legislative affairs and advocacy support, and no-cost employee speakers, and notes the ISD's dues cover the Association's cost for ISD service agreements such as Event Management services (staff, online registration, fee collection and processing, onsite event support) and Financial Services support (monthly accounting, annual tax and state report filing). Referenced but unchanged language includes Article III (Membership) Section 1, Article IV (Dues), and Article VI Section 1, which sets the board at an odd number of no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members.

Proposed Amendment 2 would ensure that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors (BOD), adding or revising language in two sections of Article IX (Committees). Under Section 3 (Committee Chairs), each standing and ad hoc committee elects a Chairperson annually from its appointed representatives; if the elected chair is not a BOD member, the Association Board appoints one of its Directors as Vice-Chair of that committee. The election is the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1, with written notice of the date, time, and place given to all appointed representatives at least seven calendar days beforehand. The rationale notes any member may chair a committee (the chair need not be a BOD member), and assigning a Director as Vice-Chair provides BOD support, ensures two-way communication between the committee and the board, and ensures compliance with BOD procedures and Association bylaws. Under Section 4 (The Government Relations Committee), a Committee Chairperson is elected annually from appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31, with each Member School District in attendance casting one vote through its appointed representative. In the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the Vice Chair position; and if the elected committee chair is not a BOD member, the Association Board appoints a Director as Vice-Chair. The extracted text of the Section 4 rationale is truncated.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A recommendation from the Troy School District high school mathematics department seeking the Board of Education's formal adoption and purchase of Precalculus for AP (©2027) by Stewart, Watson & Panman, published by Cengage Learning. The textbook is proposed as the curricular resource for both the AP Precalculus AB and AP Precalculus BC courses. The program encompasses student editions, the WebAssign digital instructional platform, a robust Teacher's Edition, and integrated AP exam preparation resources marketed as 'Fast Track to a 5.'

The rationale centers on alignment to the College Board's AP Precalculus course, which the department characterizes as focused on modeling, covariational reasoning, and functional analysis. The textbook maps to four core units: Unit 1, Polynomial and Rational Functions (developed through rate of change, behavior at the limits, and real-world modeling); Unit 2, Exponential and Logarithmic Functions (emphasizing arithmetic and geometric sequences, compounding growth, and semi-log modeling); Unit 3, Trigonometric and Polar Functions (framing periodic phenomena through circular motion, dynamic geometry, and polar coordinate systems); and Unit 4, Parametric Functions, Vectors, and Matrices (providing the linear algebra and motion foundations for advanced calculus applications).

A stated advantage is that Precalculus for AP shares its author with the district's existing AP Calculus AB and BC textbook, enabling consistent notation, language, and conceptual frameworks so students transition directly into AP Calculus AB/BC.

On learning resources, each student receives a physical classroom textbook plus digital access to the e-book and WebAssign. The department notes WebAssign lets teachers build problem sets that are structurally identical but numerically unique, intended to encourage peer collaboration on mathematical process rather than answer-sharing; for students needing differentiated support, the platform offers built-in tutorials, step-by-step guidance, and embedded instructional videos.

For exam preparation, the textbook embeds AP Practice Questions and Unit Study Guides, with each chapter concluding in AP-style multiple-choice and free-response questions to familiarize students with the exam's language and pacing; 'Fast Track to a 5' supplies targeted test preparation and full-length practice examinations. The Teacher's Edition adds pacing guides, high-yield instructional strategies for diverse learners, and differentiated activities for both extension and explicit remediation. The department concludes that adoption equips students with a mathematically rigorous resource aligned to the AP Precalculus framework and supports teachers in implementing the new AP Precalculus course.

What it is
The complete bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), provided to member school districts with proposed amendments marked (changes on pages 4, 8, and 9). Troy School District is a member district reviewing the document.

- Adopted by general membership: 1/24/2018 and 10/18/2018.

Key provisions
- Offices (Article I): principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, Oakland County, Michigan; a registered office and agent are maintained.
- Purpose (Article II): advance public education in Oakland County through cooperative efforts of elected boards, promote standards, share information, partner with Oakland Schools, and advocate for public education.

- Voting (Article III): one vote per member; each member school district has one vote on resolutions and bylaw amendments, cast in person and recorded by ballot or resolution.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The full governing bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA), distributed to member school districts—Troy School District among them—as a complete document with proposed amendments shown; a cover note directs readers to proposed changes on pages 4, 8, and 9. The adoption history records adoption by the Board of Directors on November 15, 2017; adoption by the general membership on January 24, 2018 and October 18, 2018; and amendments approved by member school districts on September 16, 2020, September 10, 2021, March 3, 2023, and June 6, 2025.

Article I (Offices) locates the association's principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, Michigan, and requires a continuously maintained registered office and registered agent.

Article II (Purpose) lists the association's aims: to advance the quality of public education in Oakland County through the cooperative efforts of locally elected boards of education; to promote high standards in educational programs and services for all students; to make information on educational issues available to board members; to conduct meetings and programs in partnership with Oakland Schools; to promote public understanding of the role of school boards and the need for citizen involvement; to enhance cooperation and communication among Oakland County boards; to present a strong voice for county school boards to political representatives; and to advocate for county, state, and national legislation supporting public education by locally elected boards.

Article III (Membership) organizes the association on a membership basis, with eligibility extended to any publicly elected Oakland County board of education member or elected Oakland ISD board member who is also in good standing with the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB). Section 2 grants each member one vote per matter, with all voting done in person; as an exception, each member school district has one vote on resolutions (Article IX) and on amending the bylaws (Article XVI), recorded upon receipt of a completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees and due before the stated deadline, with results reported to all member districts by the next general membership meeting. Section 3 permits electronic voting by the Board of Directors only for emergency business, to be reaffirmed at the next board meeting; Section 4 makes membership non-transferable and non-assignable.

Article IV (Dues) provides that the association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, by Intermediate School District membership dues not exceeding the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts.

Article V (Meeting of Members) requires an annual meeting plus not less than three additional regular membership meetings each year to appoint the Board of Directors and transact business, with the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1; special meetings may be called by the President or by two or more board members with 30 days' notice, and the Board of Directors designates meeting places. The document serves as the reference text for member districts considering the proposed 2026 amendments.

What it is
The Oakland County School Boards Association's (OCSBA) proposed 2026 bylaw updates, a two-page document circulated to member districts—including Troy School District—for consideration and vote.

Proposed Amendment 1
- Would allow a member district that pays dues directly to the association to appoint a Trustee to the Board of Directors.
- Adds language to Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Section 2 (Eligibility).
- Entitles the Intermediate School District—the only member that also pays annual dues directly (currently $6,000/year)—to appoint one Trustee to a three-year term; if the ISD declines, it must notify the board in writing within 30 days so the seat can be filled by election.
- Rationale: provides board continuity and helps fill the nine-seat working board without changing the total number of directors or the one-director-per-district limit; cites ISD in-kind support (event space, AV, legislative/advocacy support, event management, and financial services).

Proposed Amendment 2
- Would ensure that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors.
- Revises Article IX (Committees), Section 3 (Committee Chairs) and Section 4 (Government Relations Committee).
- When an elected committee chair is not a board member, the board appoints one of its Directors as committee Vice-Chair.

Purpose
Presents the proposed changes and rationale for member districts to vote on.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A two-page document titled 'OCSBA – Proposed Bylaws Updates for 2026,' prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association for its member school districts—Troy School District among them—to consider and vote on. It sets out two proposed amendments with supporting rationale and reprints related bylaw language for reference.

Proposed Amendment 1 would permit a member district that pays dues directly to the association to appoint a Trustee to a seat on the Board of Directors. The amendment adds language to Article VI (Election of Board of Directors), Section 2 (Eligibility), stating that because the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the association, it is entitled to appoint one Trustee to a three-year term on the Board of Directors; if the ISD chooses not to exercise this right, it must notify the Board of Directors in writing within 30 days of a board election so the seat can be filled by election. Existing rules—that any member is eligible and that only one member from each member school district may serve at a time—are retained. The rationale explains that, like every member district, the ISD is a member of MASB and thus of the association, but the ISD is the only member that also pays annual dues directly, currently $6,000 per year. The proposal is framed as supporting board continuity for a working board that struggles to fill all nine director positions, without altering the total number of directors or the one-director-per-district limit. It cites the ISD's financial and in-kind support: donated event space with AV equipment and staff, legislative affairs and advocacy support, no-cost employee speakers on request, and service agreements that the ISD's dues fully offset—event management (staff, online registration, fee collection and processing, and onsite support) and financial services (monthly accounting and filing annual tax and state reports).

For reference, the document reprints Article III (Membership), Article IV (Dues), and Article VI, Section 1, which provides that the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9.

Proposed Amendment 2 would ensure that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors, adding or revising language in two sections of Article IX (Committees). Revised Section 3 (Committee Chairs) provides that each standing and ad hoc committee elects a chairperson annually from the appointed representatives, and that when the elected chair is not a board member, the association board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as committee Vice-Chair; the election is the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1, with at least seven calendar days' written notice. Revised Section 4 (Government Relations Committee) provides that a chairperson is elected annually from appointed members at the first committee meeting after January 31, with each member school district in attendance casting one vote through its appointed representative; in the absence of an elected Vice-Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA assumes that role, and when the elected chair is not a board member, the board appoints one of its Directors as Vice-Chair. The rationale states that assigning a board member as Vice-Chair when the chair is not on the board provides board support for the committee, ensures two-way communication between the committee and the board, and promotes compliance with board procedures and association bylaws.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is: A resolution considered under agenda item 3.B (Recognition) at the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting on June 16, 2026, urging the Michigan Governor and Legislature to pass the 2026/2027 School Aid Budget before July 1.

Key points:
- With only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year, the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget.
- The prior year's budget was not passed until after the constitutional October 1 deadline, forcing districts to make staffing and programming decisions on speculation rather than certainty.
- Troy School District is legally obligated to complete its own budget by the end of June and will do so, but without state funding certainty may again consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff.
- The resolution argues the framework for a responsible budget already exists within three proposals under consideration.
- It urges lawmakers to keep focus on a balanced budget and to defer major reforms, including significant property tax or structural changes, to a separate debate.

Requested budget priorities: an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance; weighted funding for at-risk and English Language Learner (ELL) students; stopping the diversion of K-12 dollars away from the classroom; and fixing school safety and mental health funding.

Action: The recommended action was acceptance of the resolution, with copies to be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House and Senate and the Governor's office. The document includes standard mover/supporter and yes/no vote lines and a 'Motion declared adopted' signature block for the Board Secretary.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented as agenda item 3.B under the Recognition portion of the Troy School District Board of Education regular meeting held June 16, 2026, this is a resolution urging the Governor and the Legislature of Michigan to pass the 2026/2027 School Aid Budget by July 1st. The recommended action is acceptance of the resolution, and the document carries the standard 'Moved by,' 'Supported by,' 'Yes,' 'No,' and 'Motion declared adopted' lines signed by the Secretary of the Board of Education.

The resolution's whereas clauses lay out the district's concerns. With only two weeks remaining in the fiscal year, the Legislature had not yet passed a School Aid Budget. The prior year, the budget was not passed until after the constitutional October 1 deadline; that delay forced districts to make critical staffing and programming decisions based on speculation rather than certainty, because without a budget schools cannot responsibly plan for staffing, class sizes, transportation, or essential services. Troy School District is itself legally obligated to complete its budget by the end of June and states it will fulfill that obligation, but without certainty from Lansing on funding levels it warns it will again be forced to consider freezing programs, delaying hires, and laying off staff, causing unnecessary stress and financial concern for families and staff.

The resolution asserts that the framework for a responsible School Aid fund budget already exists within the three proposals under consideration, so there is no excuse to delay bringing those ideas together into a final agreement. It urges that focus remain on passing a responsible, balanced budget and states that this is not the time to begin discussions on major reforms; it specifically says significant property tax changes or other structural changes deserve thorough debate separate from the budget. It further states that policymakers must complete a School Aid budget that meets the needs of Michigan's students, including an inflationary increase to the foundation allowance, implementing weighted funding for at-risk and English Language Learner (ELL) students, stopping the diversion of K-12 dollars away from the classroom, and fixing school safety and mental health funding.

The operative resolving clauses call on the Legislature and the Governor to pass the School Aid Budget before July 1, and direct that a copy of the resolution be forwarded to the district's representatives in the Michigan House of Representatives and the Michigan Senate, as well as to the Governor's office.

Troy's food service is operated by Chartwells. Presenters introduced were Gayle Moran, Food Service Liaison (gmoran@troy.k12.mi.us); Nicole Gervais, Food Service Director for Chartwells (ngervais@troy.k12.mi.us); and Debbie Elzerman, Area Director for Chartwells (Deborah.Elzerman@compass-usa.com).

Meal participation data reported year-to-date: 1,471,180 meals served; 6,607 average daily lunches at 55% lunch participation; 2,637 average daily breakfasts at 22% breakfast participation; $201,570 in year-to-date a la carte revenue; and $98,598 in catering revenue.

The deck frames a 'Path Forward to Increase Lunch Participation' with several workstreams. At the secondary level for 2026-2027, 'Power Up Wednesdays' introduces new Troy protein bowls available in all secondary locations, each substitutable with tofu and/or beans: a Greek Protein Bowl (chicken, chickpeas, rice, cucumbers, tomatoes, feta, yogurt dressing), a Southwest Bowl (shaved beef, black bean and corn salsa, brown rice, marinated peppers and onions, avocado, cilantro, southwest crema), a BBQ Bowl (diced chicken, black beans, brown rice, corn, cabbage slaw, sweet potatoes, pickles, BBQ sauce), and an Asian Bowl (diced chicken, brown rice, roasted broccoli, water chestnuts, bok choy, radishes, carrots, teriyaki). Secondary participation is also driven by seasonal limited-time promotions structured around Winter, Fall, Spring, and Summer windows, plus home-made specialty pizzas, strombolis, specialty flatbreads, dips and seasonings, and pop-up sampling events such as smoothie bowls and energy bites.

At the elementary level, 'Nutrition: Game On' engages students through monthly quests featuring recipes, movement, storytelling, and hands-on activities, led by characters Leo and Dani, with Hailey Harvest (food origins), Clara Curious (science experiments), Max Motion (activity), Mei Market (smart shopping lists), and Chef Sizzle (themed recipes). Included elements are signage, overhead and countertop menu boards, engagement lessons and displays, food demos and recipe cards, and environmental refreshes (murals, fixtures, paint, flooring). Other current programs mentioned include cultural cooking competitions for middle-schoolers, student tasting and voting events, global cuisine exploration, and a farm-to-school produce program.

Meal quality and communication initiatives include summer associate trainings, a signature Culinary Masterclass led by Chartwells regional executive chefs covering 13 K-12-specific learning modules with hands-on knife-skills and food-safety instruction (all kitchen leads trained June 9 and 10), a Summer Manager Meeting, Welcome Back Orientation, and Kitchen Skills & Quality Assurance training covering USDA meal pattern requirements, food safety and sanitation, production records, menu planning, ordering, and student allergy management, with an emphasis on 'scratch and batch' cooking. Communication channels cited are a Youth Advisory Council, social media posts, monthly newsletters, up-to-date website information, Nutrislice online menus, and board reports.

The closing summary lists the overall roadmap: increasing lunch participation via secondary student meal programs and elementary 'Nutrition: Game On' in 2026-2027, ongoing meal-quality enhancement and training, equipment upgrades, smallwares refresh, and cafe refresh in fall 2026, and enhanced communications through the 2026-2027 school year.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Prepared by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) and dated May 2026, this three-page compilation presents a proposed new resolution for member-district consideration together with OCSBA's existing continuing resolutions for reference. It was included in the Troy School District Board of Education's June 16, 2026 regular meeting agenda (item 6I).

Proposed new resolution: "OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege." The stated rationale is that in the FY26 school aid budget, Section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to opt in, and that any district opting in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation - including waiving the attorney-client privilege - following a mass-casualty incident. OCSBA argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass-casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on the issue, and that nothing would stop the legislature from later tying waiver of the privilege to other funding.

The document cites OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

Continuing resolutions listed for reference, with adoption and amendment dates and cross-references to MASB resolutions, include: Accountability and Transparency, applying the same accountability, FOIA and Open Meetings standards to all publicly funded schools including ISDs, charter schools, authorizers and management companies (adopted 9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025; MASB A 6.65); Broadband Access and Devices, supporting broadband in infrastructure plans, funding for devices/software, and cybersecurity resources (adopted 9/11/2021, amended 6/5/2025; MASB A-10.30); Early Childhood, supporting universal public preschool for four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for five-year-olds (adopted 9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025; MASB A 6.15); Early On Michigan, supporting full funding of early intervention for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or risk of delay (adopted 1/26/2026); MASB A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70); Mental Health, supporting increased services and professionals and inflation-adjusted state resources (adopted 9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025; MASB G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50); https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The official 2026 Spring Resolution ballot issued by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) to its member districts, included in the Troy School District Board of Education's June 16, 2026 regular meeting agenda (item 6I).

Process described: Annually the OCSBA Government Relations Committee (GRC) establishes Legislative Priorities for the current legislative session; the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee then reviews the adopted legislative priorities and drafts resolutions based on them, referencing MASB and/or NSBA resolution information where there is alignment. After review by the Board of Directors, the proposed resolutions are presented to member districts for consideration. Under the bylaws, resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts become the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors.

Voting rules: Each member district receives one (1) vote on the proposed resolutions. The proposed resolutions, legislative priorities, and a written ballot were transmitted to member school districts on May 12, 2026. Completed ballots must be received by 5:00 PM on Friday, June 26, 2026, and emailed to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org; the document warns that the ballot must be completed, signed, and returned before the deadline or the district's vote cannot be counted. It cites OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2, which provides that member district votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees, and that votes must be received prior to the deadline.

The ballot poses the question, "Does the Board of Education approve the proposed new resolution as presented?" and provides fields for inserting the district name and the meeting date, a certification that the foregoing is a true and correct record of the vote by the Board of Education, a signature line by either the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board of Education (check one), and check boxes for YES (the Board approves the proposed new resolution as presented) or NO (the Board does not approve). Instructions direct districts to complete, sign, and email the ballot to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org no later than 5:00 PM on Friday, June 26, 2026. Questions are directed to Stefanie Crane at SCrane@Clarkston.k12.mi.us. The specific text of the proposed new resolution is not reproduced in this ballot form.

What it is
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) 2026 ballot on which member districts vote on proposed amendments to the association's bylaws. Included in Troy's June 16, 2026 agenda (item 6h).

Process
- The OCSBA Resolution & Bylaws Committee reviews the bylaws annually and recommends amendments as needed.
- Per Article XVI, Section 1, the bylaws may be altered or amended by member-district vote; the Board of Directors issues a written ballot with the proposed amendment(s), allowing at least a forty (40) day voting period; each member district has one (1) vote.

Voting
- The proposed amendments, a rationale for the change, and a written ballot were transmitted Tuesday, May 12, 2026.
- Completed, signed ballots are due by 5:00 PM Friday, June 26, 2026, emailed to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org, or the district's vote cannot be counted.
- Votes are recorded upon receipt (OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2).

Ballot structure
- Question: "Does the Board of Education approve the proposed amendments to the association bylaws?"
- Option A: one vote on all proposed changes (YES approves all changes as presented; NO approves none).
- Option B: separate votes on each proposed change - Proposal 1 and Proposal 2, each Yes/Approve or No.
- Fields for district name, meeting date, certification, and signature by the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board & Superintendent.

Note
- The full text of Proposal 1 and Proposal 2 is not included in the ballot document.

Contact
- Questions: Stefanie Crane, SCrane@Clarkston.k12.mi.us.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) 2026 member-district ballot for proposed amendments to the association's bylaws, included in the Troy School District Board of Education's June 16, 2026 regular meeting agenda (item 6h).

Process: The OCSBA Resolution & Bylaws Committee reviews the association bylaws annually and recommends amendments as needed. Once proposed amendments are reviewed by the Board of Directors, they are transmitted to member districts for consideration. The ballot cites OCSBA Bylaws Article XVI, Section 1 (Amendments), under which the bylaws may be altered or amended by the vote of the member school districts; the Board of Directors will provide a written ballot with the proposed amendment(s) to each member school district, giving at least a forty (40) day period in which to vote, and each member school district will have one (1) vote.

Voting period: The proposed amendments, a rationale for the change, and a written ballot were transmitted to every member and all member school district executive assistants on Tuesday, May 12, 2026. Completed ballots must be received by 5:00 PM on Friday, June 26, 2026, signed and emailed to OCSBAboard@ocsba-mi.org, or the district's vote cannot be counted. The ballot references OCSBA Bylaws Article III, Section 2, under which member district votes are recorded upon receipt of the completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of the district's trustees, provided they are received before the deadline.

Ballot structure: The ballot asks, "Does the Board of Education approve the proposed amendments to the association bylaws?" and provides fields for the district name, the meeting date, a certification that the foregoing is a true and correct record of the vote by the Board of Education, and a signature by either the Board Secretary or the Executive Assistant to the Board & Superintendent (check one). It offers two voting methods: Option A, one vote on all proposed changes to the bylaws (YES approves all proposed changes as presented; NO does not approve any of the proposed changes); or Option B, in which the board votes separately on each proposed change, with Proposal 1 and Proposal 2 each offering Yes/Approve or No boxes. The document instructs the board to complete one option. Questions are directed to Stefanie Crane at SCrane@Clarkston.k12.mi.us. The specific text of Proposal 1 and Proposal 2 is not reproduced in the ballot document itself.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
A memorandum on Troy School District Technology Services letterhead (4420 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098; phone 248.823.5060) from Saso Vasovski, Director of Technology, to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, regarding the 'Apple Purchase.' The memo is dated April 30, 2024, while the document/file is titled '5.20.2026 Device Refresh Proposal.' It formally requests Board of Education approval of $2,420,430 to purchase 4,400 total devices for a comprehensive refresh of both student and staff technology, framed as ensuring reliability, performance, and alignment with instructional and operational needs.

Student devices — $1,017,480: 2,400 iPads for incoming grades 2, 4, and 10, replacing all 7th-generation iPads that are end-of-life. Key actions include repurposing roughly 400 9th-generation iPads from Grade 10 to kindergarten and testing carts, reassigning current Grade 2 cart devices to Grade 3, and selling surplus 9th-generation iPads to maximize value.

Staff devices — $1,402,950: 1,000 M5 MacBook Airs and 1,000 latest-generation iPads. The stated purpose is to replace aging M1 MacBook Airs and end-of-life 7th-generation staff iPads while maintaining a 5-year refresh cycle. The district plans to retain a limited number of MacBooks for substitute/backup use and sell the remaining devices to offset cost.

Financial overview: the estimated resale offset (total estimated recovery) is $497,600–$565,600, yielding an estimated net cost of $1.85M–$1.92M. A cost table lists Student iPads at 2,400 devices / $1,017,480 / ~$423 average; Staff Devices at 2,000 / $1,402,950 / ~$701 average; and Total at 4,400 devices / $2,420,430 / ~$550 average. A resale table lists 7th-Gen iPads (3,200 units, $60–$70 each, $192K–$224K recovery), 9th-Gen iPads (800 units, $82–$92 each, $65.6K–$73.6K recovery), and M1 MacBook Air 2020 (800 units, $300–$335 each, $240K–$268K recovery).

Stated key outcomes: eliminating all end-of-life 7th-generation devices; improving performance, reliability, and user experience; maximizing value through device repurposing and resale; supporting instructional consistency and operational efficiency; and reducing future refresh costs through strategic lifecycle management. The memo closes with Vasovski's recommendation that the board approve the investment to maintain a modern, secure, and high-performing technology environment for both students and staff. The figures reconcile with the three accompanying Apple quotes: $979,000 (staff MacBook Airs) plus $423,950 (staff iPads) equals the $1,402,950 staff total, which with $1,017,480 in student iPads reaches the $2,420,430 request.

Call to order and attendance: President Anne called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Board members present were Anne, Alic, Haupt, Melton, Philippart, Potts, and Zendler. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Griffor, Keegan, Cottone, Wallace, Cronin, Griffin, Hall, Montante, Pagel, and Trudel. Outstanding Support Person of the Year: The board recognized its 2026 Outstanding Support Person of the Year, Matt Snitgen, a paraprofessional in the MOCI Room at Athens High School, nominated by Rebecca Roy. The award category spans bus drivers, secretaries, paraprofessionals, student support aides, custodial staff, food service, technology, childcare, and security; there were 25 nominees. Nomination comments praised Snitgen's belief in his students, positivity, compassion, and work ethic, and his modeling of communication through body language, gestures, facial expressions, and AAC devices; one student described a 'secret handshake' and said 'Mr. S' makes him feel happy, safe, and excited at school. His name was engraved on the Support Person Plaque to be displayed at his building for the year, and a surprise video was shown.

Legislative CAP student report: Students from the Legislative track of the district's Career Accelerator Program (CAP) presented on their study of government at the school board, city, and state legislative levels. Troy Center for Transition teacher Brynn Lawrence and International Academy East teacher Mark Chrzanowski introduced the students. Ava Pittman (IA-East) and Nathan Kohnert (Troy Center for Transition) spoke and shared a video. CAP students who shared experiences were Ayush Jaganath (Troy High), Tasnia Jannah (Athens), Sulayma Setiaarif (Athens), Aarshia Soni (Troy High), Amal Surti (IAE), Syeda Tarannum (IAE), and Harini Shrii Vengata Raghavan (Troy High).

Schools of Character recognition: Hamilton Elementary School and Troy Union Elementary School were honored as National Schools of Character, two of just 72 schools nationwide to receive the distinction from Character.org. Troy Union and Wattles were additionally recognized by Character.org as the only Michigan schools earning Promising Practices recognition, highlighting efforts that strengthen school culture, student leadership and service, positive relationships, and 'goodness in action.'

Agenda item 6.C., dated 07.21.26 and categorized as PERSONNEL, presents the extension of Superintendent Dr. Richard Machesky's contract together with the Board's public assessment of his performance. The item opens by noting that the Board recently completed the Superintendent's performance evaluation and wishes to share the resulting assessment with the community — making this document the district's public record of that evaluation rather than a purely procedural contract action.

The Board's summary states that the evaluation reflects strong, consistent confidence in Machesky's leadership across all six categories assessed.

On visionary leadership, Board members praised his work advancing the District's strategic plan while prioritizing students, inclusiveness, and instructional quality even amid difficult budget decisions. On policy and governance, his work was marked by transparency, compliance, and successful updates to key conduct codes. In instructional leadership, he was recognized for advancing a new literacy curriculum, strong professional development, and a sustained focus on core academic priorities.

Communication and community engagement were described as having shown significant improvement, with effective use of storytelling, media, and partnerships to build public trust and support. His organizational leadership was said to stand out in navigating financial challenges, specifically citing budget reduction strategies, successful contract negotiations, and on-time, on-budget bond project management. Finally, respondents consistently affirmed his professionalism, integrity, and composure, describing him as a trustworthy, student-centered leader who fosters strong relationships across the District and community.

The summary concludes that the evaluation reflects a high level of Board confidence in Dr. Machesky's leadership and supports renewal of his contract.

This contract will be in effect from July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2030, without tenure in the administrative position and subject to provisions of the written Agreement."

The four-year term running July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2030 is notably longer than the two-year terms in the companion personnel items on the same agenda. Item 6.A. extends 34 principals, assistant principals, directors, and supervisors through June 30, 2028, and item 6.B. extends four assistant superintendents — Dan Trudel, John Pagel, Kris Griffor, and Christine DiPilato — through the same June 30, 2028 date. The structure places the senior administrative team on a common two-year horizon nested inside a four-year superintendent term.
