The document follows the district's standard resolution template with blank "Moved by" and "Supported by" lines and empty Yes and No vote fields, so the agenda version records no vote outcome and no compensation terms.

The memorandum explains the procurement history. In the fall of 2025, Bid Package T3 was awarded to several contractors and included scope across multiple buildings in the district for a variety of technology and security systems. Rather than competitively rebid the new work, the district sought to maintain consistent vendor involvement for certain district-wide projects and to minimize complexity in expanding those systems. Both contractors provided quotes leveraging their existing bid pricing used in their bid submissions from the fall.

The memorandum presents the results to the administration and Board of Education for consideration, and states that upon approval by the Board of Education, change orders will be issued to each of the BP T3 contractors in the amounts shown.

- Emergency Notification and Paging Systems — VSC, Inc. — $323,919.00

The memorandum is copied to the Purchasing Department file and to Alan Wilson, Assistant Director of Technology.

The item reflects a broader pattern in the district's bond program of expanding previously competitively bid packages through change orders to incumbent contractors when additional scope arises at a building already under renovation, on the stated rationale of vendor consistency and reduced integration complexity for district-wide systems. This is the complete formal resolution supporting agenda item 8.C., captioned "TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, OAKLAND COUNTY, MICHIGAN — RESOLUTION." The companion summary resolution filed under the same item directs that this full text be included in its entirety in the official minutes of the Board meeting, which is why both versions appear in the packet.

The resolution opens with the standard recitation of meeting circumstances: a regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Oakland County, Michigan, held at the Services Center located at 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan 48098, on the 21st day of July, 2026 at 9:30 a.m., Local Time. Blank lines follow for PRESENT MEMBERS and ABSENT MEMBERS, and for the members offering and supporting the preamble and resolution.

Four WHEREAS recitals establish the rationale. First, the School District desires to lease space to house its Robotics Foundation (defined as the "Program") within, or close to, the School District's boundaries. Second, the School District has hired a real estate broker and has been searching for a location to meet the Program's needs. Third, in the interest of saving time and having the Program up and running for the 2026-2027 school year, the School District is desirous of authorizing the lease of real property consistent with the budgeted amount (defined as the "Budget") for such lease previously shared publicly at prior Board meetings. Fourth, the School District is desirous of authorizing the Superintendent, Dr. Richard Machesky, or his designee, to negotiate the terms and conditions of the Lease and enter into a Lease Agreement, as well as any and all other documents necessary and incidental to the Lease of the property for the Program on behalf of the School District, upon terms and conditions that are acceptable to the Superintendent, after consultation with legal counsel, and consistent with the Budget.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This letter, dated June 15, 2026 and addressed to the Members of the MHSAA Executive Board, requests approval of a waiver to the current cooperative team enrollment limitation to allow Troy High School and Troy Athens High School to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program beginning with the 2026-27 school year. It is submitted on behalf of the Troy School District on District Athletics letterhead showing 1522 E. Big Beaver Rd., Troy, Michigan 48083, telephone 248.823.5154, fax 248.823.5133, naming Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. as Superintendent of Schools and Matt Jansen as Director, Athletics. The letterhead carries an Equal Opportunity/Affirmative Action Employer notice.

The threshold problem is enrollment. The combined enrollment of the two high schools is 3,936 students, with Troy High School enrolling 2,127 and Troy Athens High School enrolling 1,809. The letter acknowledges directly that this total exceeds the enrollment cap established for cooperative agreements, and argues that the surrounding circumstances warrant special consideration.

The financial context is set out first. The Troy School District is described as facing a projected $12.1 million budget deficit entering the 2026-27 school year. As part of district-wide reductions, the Athletics Department has been tasked with reducing expenditures by approximately $100,000. The district recently discontinued financial support for non-MHSAA sanctioned sports, including synchronized swimming and boys and girls water polo; those programs transitioned to self-funded club status, generating approximately $50,000 in annual savings. The letter characterizes this as a difficult decision and states that additional measures are necessary to maintain sustainable athletic opportunities. A cooperative boys lacrosse program is projected to save approximately $25,000 annually.

The letter then states explicitly that the request is driven by participation numbers and program sustainability rather than solely by financial considerations, and devotes most of its length to that case. During the 2026 boys lacrosse season, Troy High School had 48 participants and Troy Athens High School had 31. Troy High School is graduating 21 seniors and Troy Athens 13, leaving projected returning participation of only 26 student-athletes at Troy High School and 15 at Troy Athens — a combined total of 41 returning players before the addition of incoming freshmen.

The situation at Athens is described as particularly concerning. Of its 15 projected returning players, only one participated at the varsity level during the 2026 season; the remaining 14 had never played lacrosse prior to that season. Although Athens attempted to field both varsity and junior varsity teams in the spring, the program was unable to consistently maintain enough healthy student-athletes to sustain junior varsity competition throughout the season. Following the 2026 season, the Troy Athens varsity boys lacrosse coach informed the district of his decision to step down, and the letter states that a significant factor in that decision was the ongoing difficulty of building and sustaining a program with limited participation numbers.

The existing arrangement is also addressed. Historically, Troy Athens participated in a cooperative arrangement with Avondale Schools, but that partnership has not provided the participation numbers necessary to sustain the program: in recent years it yielded no more than two players annually, and during the 2026 season Avondale contributed no participants. The letter concludes that this partnership is no longer a viable long-term solution.

The argument closes on educational grounds. The district contends that a fundamental goal of interscholastic athletics is to provide meaningful participation and developmental opportunities for as many student-athletes as possible, and that a cooperative program would allow both varsity and junior varsity competition to continue, ensuring beginning and developing players have an appropriate environment to learn, improve, and remain engaged. Establishing a single "Troy United" boys lacrosse program is presented as a stable structure supporting program numbers while preserving access for student-athletes from both schools.

Finally, the letter cites regional precedent, noting that within the Oakland Activities Association and surrounding communities numerous districts have been permitted to combine programs: Farmington and North Farmington, Royal Oak and Berkley, Birmingham Groves and Birmingham Seaholm, Waterford Mott and Waterford Kettering, Milford and Lakeland, and the Livonia public schools. The extracted text is truncated mid-sentence at the Livonia reference, and contains one duplicated passage characteristic of PDF text-layer extraction.

This four-year General Fund projection models Troy School District's finances from 2025-26 through 2028-29 under three scenarios, isolating two variables: whether an enhancement millage passes, and how deep annual expenditure reductions run.

The shared assumptions appear at the top. Projected Student FTE declines steadily from 12,069 in 25-26 to 11,887 in 26-27, 11,687 in 27-28, and 11,487 in 28-29 — a loss of 582 FTE, or roughly 4.8 percent, over the period. The Foundation Allowance rises from $10,836 to $11,086, $11,336, and $11,586, an increase of $442 in the first year followed by $250 per year thereafter. The two trends work against each other: per-pupil funding rises about 6.9 percent over the period while enrollment falls about 4.8 percent.

All three scenarios share identical revenue and expenditure baselines. Revenues, described as reflecting the final state budget, run $202,153,044, $193,155,509, $192,289,765, and $192,934,315. Expenditures before reductions run $207,641,522, $205,342,088, $200,197,557, and $199,847,421. Beginning fund balance for 25-26 is $33,554,567, and 25-26 closes at $28,066,089 after a net change of ($5,488,478) — a loss the district is already absorbing in the current year, identical across all three scenarios, leaving fund balance at 13.52 percent of expenditures.

Scenario 1 assumes no enhancement millage and reductions of $12,000,000 in FY27, $7,000,000 in FY28, and $7,000,000 in FY29. Net change in fund balance is ($186,579), ($907,792), and $86,894. Ending fund balance falls to $27,879,510, then $26,971,718, then recovers slightly to $27,058,612, representing 14.42 percent, 13.96 percent, and 14.03 percent of expenditures. The district very nearly holds even, but only by executing $26 million in cumulative cuts over three years, and fund balance as a share of spending never returns to a higher level.

Scenario 2 assumes the enhancement millage passes, generating $8,100,000 in 26-27, $8,334,900 in 27-28, and $8,576,612 in 28-29 — growth of roughly 2.9 percent annually — while keeping the same $12 million, $7 million, and $7 million reductions. Net change in fund balance becomes strongly positive at $7,913,421, $7,427,108, and $8,663,506. Ending fund balance rises to $35,979,510, $35,306,618, and $35,635,224, or 18.61 percent, 18.27 percent, and 18.48 percent of expenditures.

Scenario 3 assumes the millage passes with the same revenue figures but reduces the cuts after the first year: $12,000,000 in FY27, then $3,000,000 in FY28 and $3,000,000 in FY29 rather than $7,000,000 each. Net change is $7,913,421, $3,427,108, and $4,663,506. Ending fund balance reaches $35,979,510, $31,306,618, and $31,635,224, or 18.61 percent, 15.88 percent, and 16.07 percent.

Read together, the three scenarios frame a policy choice. The FY27 reduction of $12 million is common to all three and is treated as unavoidable. The enhancement millage is worth roughly $8.1 to $8.6 million annually — comparable in magnitude to the $7 million annual reduction rounds. Scenario 3 is the practical comparison: it shows that with the millage, the district could cut $4 million less per year in FY28 and FY29 than Scenario 1 requires, and still end with fund balance around 16 percent of expenditures rather than 14 percent. Without the millage, Scenario 1 shows fund balance stabilizing near 14 percent only after the full $26 million of cuts.

Regulation I, Section 1(F) caps combined enrollment at 3,500 students for boys lacrosse, while Section 1(E)(2) allows the Executive Committee to exceed the cap for two schools in the same public school district — but requires a demonstrated history of low participation and states such requests will not be approved based on financial concerns.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The MHSAA's "High School Cooperative Agreement — Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," reproducing Handbook Regulation I, Section 1 and its interpretations. Filed with Troy School District's request to form a Troy High School / Troy Athens boys lacrosse cooperative for 2026-27.

Section 1(E) — the 1,000-student baseline
Two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 1,000 students may conduct a Cooperative Program with Executive Committee approval.
- 1(E)(1): subvarsity-level co-ops may be approved regardless of enrollment, but require a demonstrated history of inadequate numbers of participants and will not be approved based on financial concerns.
- 1(E)(2): the Executive Committee may approve a co-op regardless of the combined enrollment maximum, in named sports including boys and girls lacrosse, for two or more schools of the same public school district (same governing board). Again requires a demonstrated history of low participation numbers and will not be approved based on financial concerns. Does not apply to public school academies. Case-by-case, and requires league or conference approval.

Section 1(F) — sport-specific caps
- 1(F)(1): combined enrollment up to 3,500 for sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools, a list that includes boys lacrosse
- 1(F)(2): up to 5,500 for ice hockey
- 1(F)(3): if no participating school sponsored the sport at any level the previous year, the maximum may be waived, but the agreement may not exist beyond four school years
- 1(F)(4): the cap may be exceeded for up to four years where, in the previous year, the school or its co-op dropped the sport for demonstrated lack of participation

Interpretations
Co-ops run a minimum of two years and may be voided by resolution of any cooperating board; dissolution deadlines are May 1 (fall), Aug. 15 (winter), and Oct. 15 (spring). If combined enrollment exceeds the original Division in the second year, the schools play in the higher MHSAA tournament Division.

Relevance
Troy High School (2,127) and Troy Athens (1,809) combine to 3,936, above the 3,500 lacrosse cap — which is why a waiver is sought under the same-district provision.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This document is the Michigan High School Athletic Association's reference packet titled "HIGH SCHOOL COOPERATIVE AGREEMENT — REGULATIONS, PROCEDURES AND ADVANCE PREPARATION MATERIAL TO ASSIST SCHOOLS." It reproduces MHSAA Handbook Regulation I, Section 1, together with the associated interpretations, and is filed in the July 22, 2026 Board packet alongside Troy School District's June 15, 2026 waiver request to form a cooperative boys lacrosse program between Troy High School and Troy Athens High School.

Section 1(E) establishes the general rule: in any sport, two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 1,000 students may conduct, with the approval of the Executive Committee, a Cooperative Program in the specific sports for which application has been made and approval granted.

Subsection 1(E)(1) permits the Executive Committee to approve a cooperative program at the subvarsity level only, in any sport, for two or more member high schools regardless of student enrollment. It requires a demonstrated history of inadequate numbers of participants and states the program will not be approved based on financial concerns. Students in such programs would have varsity eligibility only with their school of actual enrollment should they be brought up to a varsity team during the regular season or MHSAA Tournament. Deadlines for high school cooperative programs and the two-year minimum operating length do not apply, but the usual approvals from boards of education, the league or four future opponents, and the MHSAA Executive Committee are required.

Subsection 1(E)(2) is the provision most directly relevant to Troy's request. It permits the Executive Committee to approve a cooperative program agreement regardless of the combined student enrollment maximum, in the sports of baseball, bowling, competitive cheer, cross country, field hockey, golf, boys and girls lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, boys volleyball and wrestling, for two or more schools of the same public school district — that is, sharing the same governing board. It likewise requires a demonstrated history of low participation numbers and states the program will not be approved based on financial concerns. The allowance does not apply to public school academies. Approval is on a case-by-case basis and, as with all cooperative program applications, requires league or conference approval. Deadlines for high school cooperative programs apply.

Section 1(F) sets sport-specific enrollment ceilings. Under 1(F)(1), two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 3,500 students may conduct a Cooperative Program in specific sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools: field hockey, gymnastics, boys lacrosse, girls lacrosse, boys and girls alpine skiing, boys and girls swimming and diving, boys and girls tennis, and boys volleyball. Under 1(F)(2), the ceiling is 5,500 students for ice hockey. Under 1(F)(3), for those twelve sports, if none of the schools involved sponsored the sport at any level on an interscholastic basis during the previous school year, the 3,500 or 5,500 maximum may be waived by the Executive Committee, but the cooperative agreement may not exist beyond four school years. Under 1(F)(4), the Executive Committee may approve an agreement in excess of the 3,500 or 5,500 maximum for up to four years in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools if, during the previous year, the school or the cooperative program of which it was a part dropped the sport because of a demonstrated lack of participation; again the agreement may not exist beyond four school years.

The interpretations section addresses duration and consequences. Cooperative Programs are arrangements made for a minimum of two years but may be voided at any time by resolutions of any cooperating board of education; if voided before completion of the second year, the terminating school or schools may not enter another cooperative program in the sports involved until another two-year period has transpired. Deadlines for dissolution are May 1 for fall sports, August 15 for winter sports, and October 15 for spring sports, and changes made after those deadlines may not be reflected in tournament divisions or assignments. Agreements established under Section 1(E) whose combined enrollment later rises above 1,000 students, as established each February, are dissolved prior to the start of the school year in which the new enrollment is effective. If the combined enrollment of a Cooperative Program exceeds the original Division in the second year of an agreement, the schools will play in the higher Division of MHSAA tournaments in the sports for which there are cooperative teams. A new MHSAA member school otherwise ineligible for tournaments until its second full year may participate sooner if it becomes part of a Cooperative Program with a tournament-eligible member school. The extracted text is truncated mid-sentence in interpretation 12(e), which concerns the MHSAA Membership Resolution deadline of the fourth Friday after Labor Day.

Read against Troy's application, the regulations explain the shape of the district's argument. Troy High School's 2,127 students and Troy Athens' 1,809 combine to 3,936, exceeding the 3,500 boys lacrosse ceiling in 1(F)(1). Because both are schools of the same public school district under a single governing board, 1(E)(2) provides a route to approval regardless of the enrollment maximum — but conditions it on a demonstrated history of low participation and expressly forecloses approval based on financial concerns. That constraint appears twice in the regulation and accounts for the emphasis in the district's letter, which states that its request "is driven by participation numbers and program sustainability rather than solely by financial considerations" before detailing returning-player counts, the collapse of junior varsity competition at Athens, and the failure of the prior Avondale cooperative to supply participants.

This board narrative summary, dated June 2026 and headed "Special Education Budget Reductions — Proposed Reduction Scenario," explains the proposed special education reductions developed through the district's structured scoring process and how they connect to the broader budget plan presented to the Board.

The document opens by framing special education as one of the district's highest priorities and one of its largest areas of investment, then sets out the cost trend driving the proposals. Between 2018–2019 and 2024–2025, special education costs — covering both IEP and non-IEP services — rose from $16,744,610 to $29,210,999, an increase of $12,466,389 or 74 percent. Over the same period the special education student count grew from 1,332 to 1,367, an increase of 35 students or 3 percent. The summary identifies the gap between cost growth and enrollment growth as the central reason special education is included in the reduction scenario, describing the pace of growth as no longer sustainable within the district's structural budget.

A second driver is external: the state is leading a shift in how certain special education services are delivered, and several proposals align district staffing to new county-level service plans and county targets. The stated intent is to right-size staffing to current requirements while preserving the services students are entitled to.

The methodology is explicit. Each proposal was evaluated across six weighted criteria — impact on student learning, equity, legal and compliance risk, cost savings, feasibility, and stakeholder support — and placed into tiers based on weighted scores. Tier 1 denotes a strong candidate scoring 4.0 to 5.0; Tier 2 denotes "consider," scoring 3.0 to 3.9; Tier 3 denotes high risk requiring further study, scoring below 3.0. Savings figures reflect actual FTE and actual dollar savings as entered in the scoring matrix.

Eight proposals fall into two categories. Special Education – Classroom Instruction comprises four proposals saving $1,396,573 annually with a tier mix of two Tier 1, one Tier 2, and one Tier 3. Special Education – Non-Instructional comprises four proposals saving $1,833,312 with two Tier 1 and two Tier 2. Total proposed special education reductions are $3,229,885 across eight proposals, with a tier mix of four Tier 1, three Tier 2, and one Tier 3.

The classroom instruction proposals adjust instructional staffing to align with new county-level service plans and county staffing targets:
- Adjust Teacher Consultant and Resource Room (TC/RR) staff to meet county targets of 3.7 elementary and 3.6 secondary — $635,100 — weighted score 2.95 — Tier 3 — flagged for review
- Teacher reduction based on the new county level plan (3 L4, 1 ECP) — $348,000 — score 4.10 — Tier 1 — recommended
- Paraprofessional reduction based on the new county level plan — $236,270 — score 4.10 — Tier 1 — recommended
- Elementary Resource Room paraprofessionals reduction — $177,203 — score 3.85 — Tier 2 — consider

The TC/RR adjustment is the only Tier 3 proposal in the special education set and, at $635,100, the second-largest single item. The summary notes it carries the highest risk in the special education set and, per the scoring framework, warrants further study before adoption.

The non-instructional proposals reduce support staffing:
- Student Support Aide – General Education, reduced from 158 to 104 FTE — $1,334,362 — score 4.15 — Tier 1 — recommended
- Social Workers reduction, from 24.4 to 21.4 FTE — $348,000 — score 3.90 — Tier 2 — consider
- Psychologist reduction, from 10 to 9 FTE — $116,000 — score 3.90 — Tier 2 — consider
- Special Education Secretary — $34,951 — score 4.35 — Tier 1 — recommended

The Student Support Aide reduction of 54 FTE is described as the largest single special education reduction in the entire scenario, accounting for more than $1.3 million. The Special Education Secretary proposal carries the highest weighted score in the set at 4.35 despite being the smallest by dollar value.

On risk and planning, the summary states that of the eight proposals, four are Tier 1, three are Tier 2, and one is Tier 3. The four Tier 1 proposals total roughly $1.95 million and are described as strong candidates with low risk and high feasibility, recommended for inclusion. The three Tier 2 proposals — the Elementary Resource Room paraprofessional, social worker, and psychologist reductions — are noted as potentially benefiting from phased implementation; the extracted text is truncated partway through this discussion.

The district states that its core obligations to students with disabilities do not change: all special education programs will continue to be staffed in alignment with state and county requirements, including certified teachers, paraprofessionals, and related service providers, with decisions guided by each student's Individualized Education Program and mandated to comply with all legal and educational standards.
